events.title: Release of the first official version of the System of National Accounts (SNA 1953)
events.description: The first official version of the System of National Accounts was published, using Gross National Product (GNP) as the headline macro‑economic indicator.
events.supporting_text: The first two official versions of the System of National Accounts (1953 and 1968) used the indicator Gross National Product (GNP).

significance.justification: Shows the earliest macro‑economic metric (GNP) that later could be altered, indicating that measurement frameworks are changeable.
significance.supporting_text: The first two official versions of the System of National Accounts (1953 and 1968) used the indicator Gross National Product (GNP).

events.title: Release of the second official version of the System of National Accounts (SNA 1968)
events.description: The second official version of the System of National Accounts was issued, continuing to employ Gross National Product (GNP) as the headline indicator.
events.supporting_text: The first two official versions of the System of National Accounts (1953 and 1968) used the indicator Gross National Product (GNP).

significance.justification: Continues the historical evolution of national accounting, reinforcing that aggregate indicators can be revised.
significance.supporting_text: The first two official versions of the System of National Accounts (1953 and 1968) used the indicator Gross National Product (GNP).

events.title: Adoption of the System of National Accounts 1993 (SNA 1993)
events.description: The 1993 revision of the System of National Accounts replaced GNP with Gross Domestic Product (GDP) as the headline macro‑economic indicator.
events.supporting_text: Later on, in the SNA 1993, GDP was adopted and GNP was sidelined.

significance.justification: Marks a decisive shift from GNP to GDP, demonstrating that dominant metrics can be replaced.
significance.supporting_text: Later on, in the SNA 1993, GDP was adopted and GNP was sidelined.

events.title: Quarterly lock‑up procedure for BEA GDP reporting
events.description: A recurring, quarterly lock‑up process in which Bureau of Economic Analysis statisticians work in a secured room, isolate communications, and prepare the official GDP report that is later transmitted to the President’s Council of Economic Advisers and released to the public.
events.supporting_text: Replacing the Most Influential Indicator in the World a group of civil servants go into the "lock-up" procedure in a secure room at 4600 Silver Hill Road, Maryland, USA... This procedure is followed every quarter.

significance.justification: Illustrates the tight control and rapid dissemination of GDP data that sustains its influence on policy and markets.
significance.supporting_text: a group of civil servants go into the “lock‑up” procedure … they are not allowed to leave until they are officially dismissed.

events.title: First revision of the System of National Accounts (SNA) – 1953 edition
events.description: The inaugural revision of the international handbook that standardises the calculation of GDP, led primarily by the United Nations with a small group of active countries and experts.
events.supporting_text: The SNA has only been revised four times in the last seventy years (1953, 1968, 1993, 2008)... For the first two editions of the SNA the number of active countries/experts was small and was led only by the UN.

significance.justification: Shows the early, infrequent updates of the SNA, highlighting the slow‑changing institutional framework.
significance.supporting_text: The SNA has only been revised four times in the last seventy years (1953, 1968, 1993, 2008).

events.title: Second revision of the System of National Accounts (SNA) – 1968 edition
events.description: The second major update of the SNA, continuing the UN‑led effort to harmonise national accounting standards across participating countries.
events.supporting_text: The SNA has only been revised four times in the last seventy years (1953, 1968, 1993, 2008)... For the first two editions of the SNA the number of active countries/experts was small and was led only by the UN.

significance.justification: Illustrates the limited frequency of SNA revisions, underscoring entrenched measurement regimes.
significance.supporting_text: The SNA has only been revised four times in the last seventy years (1953, 1968, 1993, 2008).

events.title: Third revision of the System of National Accounts (SNA) – 1993 edition
events.description: The third comprehensive update of the SNA, reflecting broader international participation and evolving economic structures.
events.supporting_text: The SNA has only been revised four times in the last seventy years (1953, 1968, 1993, 2008).

significance.justification: Continues the pattern of rare updates, indicating a slow‑to‑adapt accounting system.
significance.supporting_text: The SNA has only been revised four times in the last seventy years (1953, 1968, 1993, 2008).

events.title: Release of the 2008 System of National Accounts (SNA) edition
events.description: The most recent major revision of the SNA, produced with involvement from all UN member countries and major international institutions, updating guidelines for recording economic transactions and resources.
actors: International institutes (e.g., IMF, World Bank, OECD)
events.supporting_text: The SNA was last updated in 2008... In the last revision, the SNA 2008, all countries and all the international institutes were involved.

significance.justification: The most recent, widely‑participated revision opens a window for systemic improvement.
significance.supporting_text: In the last revision, the SNA 2008, all countries and all the international institutes were involved.

events.title: Simon Kuznets' 1934 statement on the welfare interpretation of national income
events.description: Simon Kuznets, a pioneer of national accounting, publicly noted that welfare of a nation cannot be inferred from a measurement of national income, highlighting early criticism of GDP as a welfare metric.
events.supporting_text: Simon Kuznets, one of the pioneers of national accounting, famously wrote in 1934 that "the welfare of a nation ... can scarcely be inferred from a measurement of national income".

significance.justification: Shows the long‑standing critique that GDP does not capture welfare.
significance.supporting_text: Simon Kuznets... wrote in 1934 that “the welfare of a nation ... can scarcely be inferred from a measurement of national income”.

events.title: Ascendance of GDP as a national‑income innovation
events.description: The rise of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) as the dominant metric for measuring national income began in the 1930s and continued to climb the innovation curve, reaching its peak in recent decades.
events.supporting_text: The blue line shows the ascendance of GDP, which started in the 1930s and has since made a spectacular move up this innovation curve.

significance.justification: Shows how GDP has become the dominant metric, illustrating the current prevailing economic condition.
significance.supporting_text: The blue line shows the ascendance of GDP… GDP innovation is now at its peak, or very close to it.

events.title: Development of Beyond‑GDP initiatives
events.description: Initiatives that seek to replace GDP with broader measures of wellbeing and ecological health have existed for several decades and are currently on the upward part of the innovation cycle, though still far from their peak.
events.supporting_text: Beyond‑GDP initiatives have existed for several decades and are definitely on the upward curve of the innovation cycle. However, it is open for debate how high up the curve Beyond‑GDP currently is.

significance.justification: Describes an emerging alternative metric that could shift the system away from GDP.
significance.supporting_text: Beyond‑GDP initiatives have existed for several decades and are definitely on the upward curve… still far from its peak.

events.title: Adoption of the System of National Accounts (SNA)
events.description: The System of National Accounts was adopted and implemented, providing a standardized set of concepts and rules for measuring national economies and rapidly harmonising worldwide national income accounting.
events.supporting_text: The SNA has, since 1953, prescribed what concepts to use when measuring the economy. ... After the adoption and implementation of the SNA, worldwide national income accounting was harmonised rapidly.

significance.justification: Standardising national accounts creates a common framework that can be repurposed to embed natural values.
significance.supporting_text: After the adoption and implementation of the SNA, worldwide national income accounting was harmonised rapidly.

events.title: 2008 financial crisis
events.description: A global financial crisis that triggered a surge in citizens' mistrust toward economic models, policies, and data advocated by economists.
events.supporting_text: Similarly, in the wake of the 2008 crisis citizens' mistrust in the models, policies and data advocated by economists started to grow again.

significance.justification: The crisis highlighted systemic fragility and growing mistrust in economic models.
significance.supporting_text: in the wake of the 2008 crisis citizens’ mistrust in the models, policies and data advocated by economists started to grow again.

events.title: Financial crisis of 2008
events.description: The global financial crisis of 2008 triggered a crisis in macroeconomic theorising and sparked a public debate over "austerity versus stimulation" as policymakers sought ways to restore economic growth.
events.supporting_text: the financial crisis of 2008 have led to crises in macroeconomic theorising. ... most visible to the general public in the debate over "austerity versus stimulation" in the wake of the financial crisis.

significance.justification: The crisis is presented as a prevailing economic shock that destabilised macro‑economic theorising, highlighting existing systemic problems.
significance.supporting_text: financial crisis of 2008 have led to crises in macroeconomic theorising.

events.title: Publication of the Brundtland Report (Our Common Future)
events.description: Seminal publication that institutionalised the term sustainable development, defining development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
events.supporting_text: This is the underlying philosophy of the Brundtland Report which was the seminal publication that led to the institutionalisation of the term sustainable development as "development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs".

significance.justification: Introduced the concept of sustainable development, a cornerstone for re‑thinking economic metrics.
significance.supporting_text: the seminal publication that led to the institutionalisation of the term sustainable development

events.title: Adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
events.description: A list of 169 targets adopted by all UN member states, creating a powerful community around the SDGs that could be leveraged by the Beyond‑GDP movement.
events.supporting_text: a prime candidate would be the Sustainable Development Goals, a list of 169 targets that were adopted by all member states of the UN in 2015.

significance.justification: Creates a global, politically‑backed community that can mobilise actors around new well‑being metrics.
significance.supporting_text: a prime candidate would be the Sustainable Development Goals … adopted by all member states of the UN in 2015. A powerful community already exists around the SDGs

events.title: Establishment of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)
events.description: The IPCC was created in the early 1990s, leading to a coherent climate‑science community that now speaks with a common language and influences policy.
events.supporting_text: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), which started in the early 1990s, has resulted in a coherent climate science community.

significance.justification: Shows how an institutionalised scientific community can shape policy and public discourse.
significance.supporting_text: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), which started in the early 1990s, has resulted in a coherent climate science community

events.title: Publication of a Nature comment on the successor to GDP
events.description: A comment in Nature argued that, with broad participation, a new indicator to replace GDP could be completed by 2015.
events.supporting_text: A comment in Nature by some prominent voices in the Beyond-GDP movement argued in 2014 that "If undertaken with sufficiently broad participation, the hunt for the successor to GDP might be completed by 2015."

significance.justification: Raises public and scholarly attention to the need for a post‑GDP indicator.
significance.supporting_text: A comment in Nature … argued … “the hunt for the successor to GDP might be completed by 2015.”

events.title: Revision of the System of National Accounts (SNA)
events.description: A periodic revision of the SNA, historically occurring every 1–2 decades, is expected to take place sometime between 2020 and 2030.
events.supporting_text: Revision of the System of National Accounts. Historically, there has been a new SNA every 1-2 decades. That means that the next one should be expected around 2020-2030.

significance.justification: Provides a periodic opportunity to embed new well‑being and sustainability metrics.
significance.supporting_text: Revision of the System of National Accounts. Historically, there has been a new SNA every 1–2 decades

events.title: Renewal of the Sustainable Development Goals
events.description: The SDGs are expected to be discussed, evaluated and potentially renewed by the end of the 2020s, following the target to achieve the current goals by 2030.
events.supporting_text: Renewal of the Sustainable Development Goals. ... The current goals should be achieved by 2030. It is likely that by the end of the 2020s they will be discussed, evaluated and (most likely) renewed.

significance.justification: Ensures continued political commitment and coordination for beyond‑GDP initiatives.
significance.supporting_text: Renewal of the Sustainable Development Goals … will be up for renewal around that time

events.title: Long‑term process to replace GDP with the System of Global and National Accounts (SGNA) by 2030
events.description: A multi‑year, ongoing effort described in the book to develop, institutionalise and implement a new accounting framework (the SGNA) that will replace GDP as the primary metric of economic wellbeing, with full completion targeted for the year 2030.
concepts: System of Global and National Accounts (SGNA)
events.supporting_text: Part II provides the overall architecture of the strategy but, by design, this is a long‑term process that will only be fully completed by 2030.

significance.justification: The process is presented as the vehicle for moving from GDP to a new accounting system, indicating a systemic shift.
significance.supporting_text: this is a long‑term process that will only be fully completed by 2030

events.title: Publication of Simon Kuznets Report to Congress
events.description: A landmark report on national income statistics prepared by Simon Kuznets was submitted to the U.S. Congress, providing macro‑economic data requested during the Great Depression.
events.supporting_text: a landmark publications in the history of national accounting: a report by Simon Kuznets on 4 January 1934.

significance.justification: Shows the reliance on macro‑economic data during the Great Depression, highlighting the prevailing focus on GDP‑type statistics.
significance.supporting_text: The report ... contained estimates for economic activity which the US Congress requested as a result of the Great Depression.

events.title: Adoption of Resolution 220 Requesting National Income Statistics
events.description: The U.S. House of Representatives voted for Resolution 220, which formally requested the Department of Commerce to compile national income statistics for the period 1932‑1932.
events.supporting_text: it took until 8 June 1932 before La Follette could get a majority to vote for resolution 220 which requested national income statistics for the period 1992-1932.

significance.justification: Illustrates the emerging demand for national income data, exposing the existing scarcity of such statistics.
significance.supporting_text: La Follette could get a majority to vote for resolution 220 which requested national income statistics for the period 1992–1932.

events.title: Bretton Woods Conference
events.description: An international conference held at Bretton Woods that established the post‑war monetary system, creating the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank.
locations: Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, United States
events.supporting_text: The international economic order changed significantly at the Bretton Woods meeting in 1944, ushering in a new economic era with the gold standard being replaced by a system in which currencies were pegged to the US dollar.

significance.justification: Established a new post‑war economic order centred on growth‑oriented institutions.
significance.supporting_text: The international economic order changed significantly at the Bretton Woods meeting in 1944, ushering in a new economic era.

events.title: Founding of the Organisation for European Economic Co‑operation (OEEC)
events.description: The OEEC was created to administer the Marshall Plan aid and to coordinate European economic recovery after World War II.
events.supporting_text: Initially called the Organisation for European Economic Co‑operation (OEEC), it was founded in 1948 and played an important role in the post‑war economic recovery of Europe.

significance.justification: Created a coordinated body to manage post‑war economic recovery across Europe.
significance.supporting_text: It was founded in 1948 and played an important role in the post‑war economic recovery of Europe.

events.title: Establishment of the United Nations
events.description: The United Nations replaced the League of Nations as the primary international organization for peace, security, and cooperation.
events.supporting_text: The ineffective League of Nations was replaced by the United Nations in 1945.

significance.justification: Provided a global platform for coordination, including later statistical cooperation.
significance.supporting_text: The ineffective League of Nations was replaced by the United Nations in 1945.

events.title: Signing of the North Atlantic Treaty (NATO)
events.description: The North Atlantic Treaty was signed, establishing the NATO alliance for collective defense among Western nations.
events.supporting_text: In 1949, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) was agreed.

significance.justification: The text mentions NATO without linking it to economic metrics or nature‑related outcomes.
significance.supporting_text: In 1949, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) was agreed.

events.title: Founding of the European Economic Community
events.description: The European Economic Community (EEC) was established as a forerunner of the European Community, promoting economic integration among its members.
events.supporting_text: The European Economic Community, a forerunner of the European Community, was founded in 1957.

significance.justification: No explicit connection to the initiative of harmonising with nature is provided.
significance.supporting_text: The European Economic Community, a forerunner of the European Community, was founded in 1957.

events.title: Implementation of the Marshall Plan
events.description: A large‑scale U.S. economic assistance programme (1948‑1952) that provided aid to rebuild European economies and stimulated the production of national accounts in recipient countries.
events.supporting_text: The Marshall Plan, which ran from 1948 to 1952, was a large‑scale economic programme designed to put Europe on the road to economic prosperity and peace.

significance.justification: A large‑scale aid programme that coordinated resources across nations.
significance.supporting_text: The Marshall Plan ... was a large‑scale economic programme designed to put Europe on the road to economic prosperity and peace.

events.title: United Nations Begins Collecting National Accounts Data
events.description: The UN started systematic collection of national accounts statistics from member countries, expanding the global data base for GDP measurement.

events.supporting_text: The second source is the United Nations, which started to collect national accounts data in 1952.

significance.supporting_text: The United Nations, which started to collect national accounts data in 1952.

events.title: Publication of the First Edition of the System of National Accounts (SNA)
events.description: The inaugural edition of the SNA was released, providing an internationally agreed framework for compiling national income and product accounts.
events.supporting_text: Macroeconomic statistics started to harmonise into the System of National Accounts, with the first edition being published in 1953.

significance.justification: Introduced a systematic framework that could be adapted for broader measurement purposes.
significance.supporting_text: Macroeconomic statistics started to harmonise into the System of National Accounts, with the first edition being published in 1953.

events.title: OECD Pledges 50 % GDP Increase for Member Countries by 1970
events.description: The OECD set an international growth target, committing its members to raise aggregate GDP by half within the next decade.
actors: OECD (Organisation for Economic Co‑operation and Development)
events.supporting_text: In 1961, this target setting was elevated to an international goal: the OECD pledged a 50 per cent increase in GDP of OECD countries by 1970.

significance.justification: Shows the explicit policy focus on GDP growth as a primary objective.
significance.supporting_text: In 1961, the OECD pledged a 50 per cent increase in GDP of OECD countries by 1970.

events.title: Publication of John Maynard Keynes’ *The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money*
events.description: Keynes released his seminal work that founded modern macroeconomics and reshaped the theoretical basis for national income accounting.
events.supporting_text: A hugely influential publication of 1936 was by John Maynard Keynes, one of the defining figures in twentieth‑century economics. In *The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money*, Keynes laid the foundation for macroeconomics...

significance.justification: Provided a foundational macro‑economic theory that reshaped economic thinking.
significance.supporting_text: Keynes ... laid the foundation for macroeconomics and still has great influence today.

events.title: Publication of Wassily Leontief’s First Input‑Output Paper
events.description: Leontief introduced the input‑output model for the United States, a methodological breakthrough that later influenced the System of National Accounts.
events.supporting_text: Wassily Leontief published his first paper on input‑output economics, in which a model that linked the economic input to the outputs was created for the United States for the year 1919.

significance.justification: Introduced a model linking economic inputs and outputs, revealing systemic interdependencies.
significance.supporting_text: Leontief published his first paper on input–output economics, in which a model that linked the economic input to the outputs was created.

events.title: Publication of Jan Tinbergen’s First Econometric Work
events.description: Tinbergen released his initial econometric study of business‑cycle analysis, contributing to the quantitative foundations of national accounting.
events.supporting_text: In 1936, Jan Tinbergen also published his first work, in which he produced an econometric model for business cycle analysis.

significance.justification: Presented econometric modelling that exposed dynamic relationships within the economy.
significance.supporting_text: Tinbergen also published his first work, in which he produced an econometric model for business cycle analysis.

events.title: Adoption of floating exchange rates by Japan and European countries
events.description: In 1973 Japan and European countries stopped using the Bretton Woods framework, replacing fixed exchange rates tied to the dollar with floating currencies.
events.supporting_text: By 1973 Japan and European countries effectively stopped using the Bretton Woods framework, replacing exchange rates fixed to the dollar with floating currencies.

significance.justification: Shows a systemic monetary shift away from the fixed‑rate Bretton Woods regime.
significance.supporting_text: By 1973 Japan and European countries effectively stopped using the Bretton Woods framework, replacing exchange rates fixed to the dollar with floating currencies.

events.title: Robert Lucas's presidential address to the American Economic Association
events.description: Robert Lucas delivered his presidential address to the American Economic Association, asserting that macroeconomics had solved the problem of depression prevention.
events.supporting_text: Robert Lucas, Nobel Prize winner and founder of the new classical school, said during his presidential address to the American Economic Association in 2003: "My thesis in this lecture is that macroeconomics in this original sense has succeeded: Its central problem of depression prevention has been solved, for all practical purposes, and has in fact been solved for many decades."

significance.justification: Reinforces confidence in growth‑centric macroeconomics, discouraging alternative wellbeing metrics.
significance.supporting_text: Robert Lucas ... said ... “macroeconomics ... has succeeded ... depression prevention has been solved”.

events.title: Publication of "The State of Macro" paper
events.description: Olivier Blanchard published a paper titled "The State of Macro" in which he declared that the state of macroeconomics was good and that there was a broad convergence of vision.
events.supporting_text: In a 2008 paper titled "The State of Macro" Olivier Blanchard, who later was the chief economist at the IMF, declared that "the state of macro is good" and that there was a "broad convergence of vision".

significance.justification: Declares macroeconomics as “good”, bolstering the status‑quo of GDP‑focused policy.
significance.supporting_text: In a 2008 paper titled “The State of Macro” Olivier Blanchard ... declared that “the state of macro is good”.

events.title: Fall of the Berlin Wall

The fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of the communist system reinforced the perception that capitalist democracies were the superior form of governance.

events.title: Student protests across the western world

events.title: Great Moderation period
events.description: A period that began in the mid‑1980s during which key economic variables such as GDP growth, industrial production, unemployment and inflation showed reduced volatility, a trend credited to Alan Greenspan’s leadership of the Federal Reserve.

significance.supporting_text: Alan Greenspan ... credited with the “Great Moderation”, a period ... when economic variables ... began to decline in volatility.

events.title: Contested Hegemony period
events.description: A historical phase from 1973 to 2008 characterized by growing criticism of GDP as a measure of welfare, shifts in economic paradigms, and contested dominance of different schools of economic thought.
events.supporting_text: Contested Hegemony (1973 - 2008) ... The criticism from other domains grew significantly in the period of "contested hegemony".

significance.supporting_text: the criticism from other domains grew significantly in the period of “contested hegemony”.

significance.supporting_text: In the autumn of 1945, a subcommittee was initiated under the chairmanship of Richard Stone.

events.title: Publication of 1947 subcommittee report on national accounts
events.description: The subcommittee produced a report that is regarded as the start of the harmonisation process of the System of National Accounts.

events.title: Update of SNA handbook (1968)

events.title: Harmonisation process of the System of National Accounts
events.description: A multi‑year effort that began with the 1947 subcommittee report and culminated in the 1993 worldwide agreement, spanning 46 years of international coordination and standardisation.

significance.supporting_text: Taking the report of the 1947 subcommittee as the starting point of the harmonisation process, it took forty‑six years to reach full worldwide harmonisation.

events.title: John F. Kennedy convinces OECD to set growth target for member countries
events.description: President John F. Kennedy was instrumental in persuading the Organisation for Economic Co‑operation and Development (OECD) to adopt a quantitative growth target for all OECD members.
events.supporting_text: John F. Kennedy was instrumental in convincing the OECD to set a growth target for all OECD countries in 1961.

significance.justification: The event promoted a GDP growth target, reinforcing a metric that ignores ecological wellbeing.
significance.supporting_text: John F. Kennedy was instrumental in convincing the OECD to set a growth target for all OECD countries in 1961.

events.title: OECD pledges to increase GDP by 50 % by 1970
events.description: In the same year, the OECD formally pledged that member economies would raise their gross domestic product by half of their 1961 level by the year 1970.
events.supporting_text: In that year, the OECD pledged to increase GDP in OECD countries by 50 per cent in 1970.

significance.justification: A formal commitment to boost GDP entrenches the dominance of a growth‑centric metric.
significance.supporting_text: OECD pledged to increase GDP in OECD countries by 50 per cent in 1970.

events.title: Robert Kennedy speech criticizing GDP
events.description: Robert Kennedy delivered a widely quoted speech denouncing the Gross National Product (GNP) as an inadequate measure of societal wellbeing, pointing out its omission of health, education, environmental quality, and other non‑material values.
events.supporting_text: In 1968, Robert Kennedy gave one of the most eloquent of speeches to argue against GDP (or rather GNP at the time): "Too much and for too long, we seemed to have surrendered personal excellence and community values in the mere accumulation of material things..."

significance.justification: The speech publicly challenged GDP’s adequacy, shifting discourse toward broader wellbeing values.
significance.supporting_text: Robert Kennedy gave one of the most eloquent of speeches to argue against GDP...

events.title: Update of the Compendium of Sustainable Development Indicator Initiatives
events.description: The Compendium of Sustainable Development Indicator Initiatives, the largest database of Beyond‑GDP initiatives, was updated up to the year 2011 before being taken offline.
events.supporting_text: The biggest database, the Compendium of Sustainable Development Indicator Initiatives, listed around 900 initiatives all around the world but not all of these are at the national level.2 ... Note that the Compendium was updated up to 2011 and has since been taken offline.

significance.justification: An updated compendium would list many more initiatives, showing the growing scope of alternative metrics.
significance.supporting_text: If it had continued after 2011, it is clear that there would be significantly more entries.

events.title: Compendium of Sustainable Development Indicator Initiatives taken offline
events.description: After its 2011 update, the Compendium was removed from public access and is no longer maintained online.
events.supporting_text: Note that the Compendium was updated up to 2011 and has since been taken offline.

significance.justification: Taking the database offline reduces visibility and hampers coordination of Beyond‑GDP efforts.
significance.supporting_text: Compendium of Sustainable Development Indicator Initiatives taken offline.

events.title: Initiation of Subjective Well‑being (SWB) measurement programmes
events.description: The systematic measurement of subjective well‑being began shortly after World War II and has expanded steadily across an increasing number of countries.
events.supporting_text: The measurement of SWB started just after the war and the number of countries has shown steady growth ever since.

significance.justification: The start and steady growth of SWB measurement indicate a shift toward alternative wellbeing metrics.
significance.supporting_text: The measurement of SWB started just after the war and the number of countries has shown steady growth ever since.

events.title: Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment
events.description: The first global UN conference on the environment, which institutionalised environmental concerns and led to the creation of UNEP.
events.supporting_text: First, the Green Movement had emerged in the 1950s/1960s but the Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm institutionalised environmental concerns. It was the first global UN conference on the environment and was highly influential at the time.

significance.justification: The conference institutionalised environmental concerns, creating a systemic shift toward integrating nature in policy.
significance.supporting_text: the Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm institutionalised environmental concerns. It was the first global UN conference on the environment and was highly influential at the time.

events.title: Establishment of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP)
events.description: UNEP was created as a direct outcome of the Stockholm Conference, stimulating governments worldwide to set up environmental ministries.
locations: United Nations Headquarters, New York, USA
events.supporting_text: The conference had a significant effect on the institutionalisation of environmental issues. It created the United Nations Environmental Programme, which stimulated governments all over the world to set up environmental ministries.

significance.justification: UNEP spurred governments worldwide to create environmental ministries, enabling coordinated action.
significance.supporting_text: It created the United Nations Environmental Programme, which stimulated governments all over the world to set up environmental ministries.

events.title: Publication of Limits to Growth
events.description: Seminal report of the Club of Rome that raised environmental awareness by modelling resource depletion and exponential growth limits.
events.supporting_text: 1972 was also the year that the seminal Limits to Growth report of the Club of Rome was published. This report played a major role in raising environmental awareness.

significance.justification: The report raised public awareness of ecological limits and the unsustainability of endless growth.
significance.supporting_text: 1972 was also the year that the seminal Limits to Growth report ... played a major role in raising environmental awareness.

events.title: OECD programme "The problems of modern society"
events.description: A multi‑year OECD programme (1968‑1974) aimed at solving social problems linked to rapid economic growth, later sidelined as focus returned to GDP growth.
actors: Organisation for Economic Co‑operation and Development (OECD)
events.supporting_text: It is no wonder that the OECD, the bastion of economic growth after the Second World War, set up a programme to solve "The problems of modern society", which ran from 1968 to 1974.

significance.justification: The programme highlighted that rapid post‑war economic growth did not automatically improve societal wellbeing.
significance.supporting_text: the OECD ... set up a programme to solve “The problems of modern society” ... it was becoming abundantly clear that spectacular economic growth ... did not automatically create a better society.

events.title: Publication of Our Common Future (Brundtland Report)
events.description: United Nations World Commission on Environment and Development report that popularised the term “sustainable development”.
actors: United Nations World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED)
events.supporting_text: The real game‑changer in Beyond‑GDP measurement was the seminal publication by the United Nations World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED) in 1987. The commission's report, Our Common Future, is often referred to as the "Brundtland Report".

significance.justification: The report introduced and popularised “sustainable development,” providing a new framework for systemic change.
significance.supporting_text: The commission’s report, Our Common Future ... led to the popularisation of the term “sustainable development”... It provided a narrative to speak about global environmental issues.

events.title: 1992 Rio Earth Summit
events.description: United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (Earth Summit) in Rio de Janeiro that institutionalised the term “sustainable development” and adopted Agenda 21.
events.supporting_text: The term "sustainable development" was further institutionalised due to the "Earth Summit" in Rio de Janeiro in 1992. ... At this conference, Agenda 21 was adopted which included a recommendation for countries to monitor their progress towards sustainable development.

significance.justification: The summit institutionalised sustainable development, creating an international platform for coordinated action.
significance.supporting_text: the “Earth Summit” in Rio de Janeiro in 1992 ... institutionalised the term “Sustainable Development”.

events.title: Creation of the Measure of Economic Welfare (MEW)

significance.supporting_text: A different, rather unique, approach was proposed in 1974 by Roefie Hueting: Sustainable National Income.

significance.supporting_text: The MEW methodology inspired the Index for Sustainable Economic Welfare (ISEW), which was proposed in 1989 by Daly and Cobb.

events.title: Publication of Costanza et al. paper likening GDP growth to addiction
events.description: Costanza and colleagues (2017) published a novel paper that compares society’s focus on economic growth to an addiction and explores how motivational interviewing techniques might be applied to reduce the ‘addiction’ to GDP.
events.supporting_text: In a novel paper, Costanza et al. (2017) liken society's focus on economic growth to a real addiction. They explore how methods that are used for addicts might be adopted at the societal level. For example, Motivational Interviewing (MI) is based on engaging addicts in a positive discussion of their goals, motives and futures.

significance.justification: Frames GDP growth as an addiction and proposes applying Motivational Interviewing, suggesting a novel pathway for change.

concepts.name: Sustainable development
concepts.definition: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs; it stresses the wellbeing of the current generation and the wellbeing of future generations.
key_proponents: United Nations World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED)
concepts.supporting_text: This is the underlying philosophy of the Brundtland Report which was the seminal publication that led to the institutionalisation of the term sustainable development as "development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs".

Sustainable Development

By the end of the 1980s a new concept which linked economic, environmental and social issues emerged. The term "sustainable development", which was popularised by the Brundtland Report, has become ubiquitous ever since.

This report led to the popularisation of the term "sustainable development". Ever since then, sustainable development has been a catch‑all term which defines societal progress as the balanced development of the economic, environmental and social dimensions of society.
This is sometimes seen by economists as the conceptual equivalent of the term "sustainable development".
